nature-es-043.title: Well-being: how well a life is going
nature-es-043.text: Money and medicine can make a life better, yet neither is itself a good life. They are causes. The thing they cause is well-being: what is good for a person in itself, a measure of how well their life is going for them. It is also called welfare or quality of life. Broadly, it weighs all the good and bad in a life; narrowly, it means only the good, in contrast to ill-being. Philosophers have argued about it since antiquity, when its study began as discussions of how to live a good life. Some agreement has emerged. Positive emotions, achievements, relationships and health usually contribute to it. Well-being can be judged for a person or for a whole community, whose well-being has economic, social, environmental and cultural sides. Welfare economics studies how economic activity affects it, comparing policies with metrics such as income distribution, GDP and consumer surplus. Nature enters the picture here. Defenders of {{ref:nature-val-059}}, the view that puts humans at the center, argue that a healthy environment matters because human well-being needs it, not for its own sake.

nature-es-026.title: Recreation: the human need to play
nature-es-026.text: Leisure is a human right under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Recreation is what people do with it: activity for enjoyment, amusement or pleasure. The urge for it is treated as a basic part of human biology and psychology. It needs leisure, meaning time free from work, sleep, daily chores and social duties. Affluence, population trends and a growing commercial supply have raised recreation's role in modern life. Parks and beaches are key venues, and the tourism industry has recognized that many visitors come for recreation itself. That makes it an ecosystem service. Recreation and tourism are among the cultural services ecosystems provide, alongside spiritual fulfillment. When biodiversity is lost, ecosystems can no longer offer the same places to play.

nature-es-034.title: Outdoor recreation: a $696.7 billion slice of the economy
nature-es-034.text: In 2024 outdoor recreation accounted for $696.7 billion of value added, 2.4 percent of US GDP, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis. Outdoor recreation is leisure done outdoors, usually in natural settings. It runs from fishing, hunting and walking to hiking, camping, climbing, kayaking and skiing. People pursue it for exercise, general well-being and spiritual renewal, with less stress on competition than organized sport. It often happens in thinly populated country with mountains, lakes, rivers and scenic views. The benefits are measurable: university outdoor programs have been shown to help students' well-being and stress levels. Forest managers now count outdoor recreation among the objectives forests serve, alongside timber, conservation and hunting.

nature-es-022.title: Biophilia: an inborn love of living things?
nature-es-022.text: Why do people keep houseplants, care for animals, and sometimes risk their lives to save them? The biophilia hypothesis offers an answer: humans have an inborn urge to seek connection with nature and other living things. Erich Fromm first used the word and treated it as a biologically normal instinct. Edward O. Wilson introduced and popularized the hypothesis in his 1984 book Biophilia. Evolutionary psychology supplies a reason: ancestors with closer ties to nature may have found food, water and shelter more easily. If so, modern cities may poorly suit minds that evolved in natural settings, as research suggests. The opposite also exists. Biophobia is an inherited fear of nature and animals, such as fear of snakes and spiders. Conservationists worry that losing the connection could breed disregard for wild species and speed ecosystem loss, so reconnecting people with nature has become a conservation goal. The idea also inspires biophilic cities, whose extra green space can double as wildlife corridors.

nature-es-036.title: Subjective well-being: asking people how happy they are
nature-es-036.text: The most common way to measure happiness is also the simplest: ask. Subjective well-being is well-being, or happiness, as judged by the people living the lives in question rather than by an outside observer. Ed Diener defined it by three signs: frequent positive feelings, infrequent negative ones, and judgments such as life satisfaction. Its components are affect (emotions and moods), life satisfaction, and eudaimonia, a sense of meaning and purpose. Researchers usually measure it by self-report, often with life-satisfaction questionnaires. Definitions typically leave out objective conditions such as wealth or health, though these can sway ratings. Top-down theories trace it to stable personality; bottom-up theories build it from happy experiences and met needs. The quality of social ties matters far more than their number. Nature matters too: a person's felt connection with nature directly raises affect and life satisfaction. {{ref:nature-acct-019}} often uses the measure to judge whole populations.

nature-es-015.title: The aesthetics of nature: why landscapes move people
nature-es-015.text: In 2017 Andrew Lothian's The Science of Scenery tried to measure scenic beauty by asking the public to rate landscape photographs. Critics said the method favored picture-postcard views and ignored the bodily experience of being in a place. The aesthetics of nature is the branch of philosophy that studies natural things for their beauty and other aesthetic qualities. It is one branch of {{ref:nature-val-065}}. Its main ideas took shape in the 18th and 19th centuries, among them positive aesthetics and disinterestedness, meaning judging something while setting aside personal and practical interests. Beauty carried moral weight for {{ref:nature-hist-051}}. He named integrity, stability and beauty as the three features of ecosystems that give rise to a {{ref:nature-val-049}}. Science has added a twist. Fractal patterns that echo nature can make built spaces more soothing to look at, and people prefer particular levels of their complexity.

nature-es-017.title: Nature connectedness: when nature is part of who you are
nature-es-017.text: People who count nature as part of their identity are more likely to join environmental groups and call themselves environmentalists. Nature connectedness is how far a person counts nature as part of who they are. It behaves like a personality trait, fairly stable over time and across situations, yet it can grow after time spent outdoors. Schultz split it into three parts: feeling at one with nature, caring for it, and committing to protect it. Highly connected people report higher psychological and social well-being. A meta-analysis, a study combining many studies, confirmed a strong correlation with pro-environmental behavior but found a weaker causal role than the correlations suggested. Even so, raising people's connection to nature may motivate green behavior more effectively than laws and rules. That matters to planners, because more contact with nature and easier access to city green space may raise both well-being and ecological behavior.

nature-es-033.title: Nature tourism: traveling to see the wild
nature-es-033.text: Stargazers, cyclists and birdwatchers all travel for the same basic reason. Nature tourism is travel to enjoy an area's natural attractions, including its plants and animals. It overlaps with wildlife and adventure tourism, and it includes {{ref:nature-es-012}}, which focuses on environmental education and conservation. Parks set aside by nations have become closely tied to it. Its effects cut both ways. Visitors can harm the places they come to see. Yet tourism can also aid conservation, by making the remaining natural areas more valuable to local people and landowners.

nature-es-038.title: Sustainable tourism: can travel last?
nature-es-038.text: Tourism is one of the world's largest and fastest-growing industries, and its growth will put heavy stress on the remaining biodiverse habitats and Indigenous cultures. Sustainable tourism is the attempt to manage that. It attends to tourism's economic, social and environmental effects while improving visitors' experiences and meeting host communities' needs. The movement emerged after the environmental awareness of the 1960s and 1970s, amid growing mass tourism, and grew out of {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. Done well, it brings local jobs, development and infrastructure. In fragile or remote areas, the number of visitors a place can bear is a key concern. Tourism's reliance on fossil fuels ties it to sustainable transport and climate change. The Global Sustainable Tourism Council's GSTC Criteria are the international standard for certifying businesses. The term remains open to many readings, and critics call it a contradiction: tourism is extractive, they argue, and cannot continue indefinitely.

nature-es-012.title: Ecotourism: travel that is supposed to help
nature-es-012.text: In South Africa, 70% of the money the {{ref:nature-gov-148}} system makes comes straight from tourism. That is the promise of ecotourism: travel to natural places that aims to do little harm and to support conservation and environmental education. Some definitions add that it must pay its way for the host community or make conservation financially possible. It counts as one part of sustainable tourism. It differs from plain nature tourism by trying to build tourists' appreciation of habitats and local culture. The possible benefits are real: visitor spending and jobs, money to run and expand {{ref:nature-gov-038}}, and a reason to protect or restore natural land. So are the drawbacks. Visitors can still damage the places they protect, raise local rents and property values, and bring health risks to people and wildlife. Most ecotourism businesses belong to foreign investors, so most profits leave the area instead of returning to the local economy or conservation. The trips usually depend on flying, which adds to climate change, and few operators leave a net-positive mark on the environment. Weak regulation lets underwater hotels and helicopter tours call themselves ecotourism, a form of {{ref:nature-nbs-075}}. Environmentalists, interest groups and governments define the term differently, and where tourism stops being ecotourism is still disputed.

nature-es-014.title: Underdevelopment tourism: when the profits fly away
nature-es-014.text: Ecotourism is meant to benefit local people, but critics see a different pattern. Underdevelopment tourism is the idea that multinational companies control ecotourism development and take most of its gains, leaving local communities without ownership. It can limit local control over land, water and wildlife and raises questions about who shares tourism's benefits. Large corporate projects can also cause heavy environmental damage, loss of traditional culture and exploitation of local workers.

nature-es-044.title: Three theories of what makes a life go well
nature-es-044.text: Jeremy Bentham, father of classical utilitarianism, proposed a felicific calculus to measure and add up pleasure and pain. His view, hedonism, holds that pleasure and pain are the only factors of well-being. Desire theories disagree: people fare well when they get what they want. Objective list theories add items such as health, friendship, achievement, knowledge and autonomy. These benefit a person whether or not that person cares about them.

nature-es-031.title: Green space and the mind
nature-es-031.text: An eighteen-year Danish study found that children raised with the most green space had 55% less risk of developing several psychiatric disorders. Research like this examines the link between time in natural surroundings and mental health. Exposure can be almost any contact with nature: a hike, a forest visit, a walk in a park, time by a lake. Contact with nature is tied to lower stress, better mood, more happiness and meaning, and less mental distress. A 10-year UK study found that greener surroundings within 300m of home, and nearby green and blue spaces, both lowered the risk of anxiety and depression. The mind sharpens too. Nature exposure improves working memory, attention and mental flexibility, while urban settings have been linked to attention deficits. Even a glimpse helps. Students who saw a flowering roof garden for 40 seconds made fewer errors on a dull task than those shown a concrete roof. Modern indoor, screen-heavy lives have cut that contact, and therapists now use nature in treatments called ecotherapy.

nature-es-025.title: Attention restoration: how nature rests a tired mind
nature-es-025.text: Drifting clouds and flowing water hold attention without demanding it. Stephen and Rachel Kaplan called this soft fascination, and it is the core of attention restoration theory. The theory holds that time in nature, or even a view of it, helps people recover from the mental tiredness of sustained, deliberate focus. Busy modern settings tax directed attention, which can run down into attention fatigue. Nature lets that effortful attention rest. A restorative setting has four properties: being away, extent, compatibility and fascination. The theory builds on William James's distinction between effortful voluntary attention and automatic involuntary attention. It has a rival. Roger Ulrich's Stress Reduction Theory says nature helps through emotional and physical responses, not mental ones.

nature-es-020.title: Nature therapy: forests as medicine
nature-es-020.text: In 1982 Tomohide Akiyama, head of Japan's ministry in charge of forests, popularized forest bathing, or shinrin-yoku, to get more people into the woods. It is one form of nature therapy, also called ecotherapy: a broad group of treatments that use time in nature to improve mental or physical health. Forest therapy and Sami Lok are others. The effects are usually tied to stress recovery, since contact with nature lowers cortisol, a stress hormone, and heart rate. Contact with nature is also linked to fewer depressive symptoms. Qing Li's small trials from 2005 tested forest walks of a few hours a day. They raised natural killer cells, part of the immune system, by roughly 50 percent; city walks did not. The therapy is cheap and accessible, needing only parks, shared gardens or other public outdoor space. The evidence is less settled than the enthusiasm. Results vary with study design, and many studies rely on self-reports. Reviews disagree on how strong the case is, and some call it inconclusive and ask for larger trials.

nature-es-028.title: Sense of place: why some places feel like home
nature-es-028.text: The places of childhood become a primal landscape, part of a person's identity and a yardstick for judging places later in life. Sense of place is the many-sided relationship between people and places, covering what makes a place special and the attachment people feel to it. Some treat it as a quality certain places have; others see it as a feeling held by people. It need not be positive: geographer Yi-Fu Tuan pointed to senses of place rooted in fear. Places with a strong sense of place have an identity deeply felt by residents and visitors, and World Heritage listing tries to protect them. Losing such places hurts. Climate-driven damage to valued places can bring grief and solastalgia, a distress at environmental change close to home. Many Indigenous cultures are losing their sense of place to climate change. Contact with natural environments strengthens social ties, care for land and sense of place.

nature-es-030.title: Cultural landscapes: where people and nature made each other
nature-es-030.text: In 2009 the Dresden Elbe Valley was removed from the World Heritage list after a four-lane highway was built across the Elbe. It had been listed as a cultural landscape: a landscape shaped by the long interplay of human activity and the natural environment. Geographer Otto Schlüter first used the term academically in the early 20th century, contrasting original landscape with landscape made by culture. Carl O. Sauer's classic definition is neat: culture is the agent, the natural area is the medium, and the cultural landscape is the result. In 1992 the World Heritage Committee began revising its guidelines so places neither purely natural nor purely cultural could be listed. It sorts them into three kinds: landscapes designed by people, organically evolved landscapes, and associative landscapes valued for religious, artistic or cultural ties. New Zealand's Tongariro became the first listed under these criteria, in 1993; its mountains hold spiritual meaning for the Maori.

nature-es-027.title: Therapeutic recreation: play as treatment
nature-es-027.text: Therapeutic recreation is a profession that uses recreation's health benefits as a form of therapy. It is used in rehabilitation, in youth and adult psychiatric care, and in caring for elderly, disabled and chronically ill people. In the United States, practitioners certified by the NCTRC are called Certified Therapeutic Recreation Specialists.

nature-es-040.title: Nature positive tourism: leaving places better
nature-es-040.text: The World Travel and Tourism Council says 80% of goods and services in the industry are highly dependent on nature. Nature positive tourism aims not just to leave no trace but to leave positive benefits for the natural world. It is a form of regenerative tourism, meant to help reverse nature's decline by 2030 and achieve full recovery by 2050. Actions include supporting tree replanting, making room for nature in city hotels, and cutting light and water pollution.

nature-es-039.title: Responsible tourism: everyone is accountable
nature-es-039.text: Responsible tourism is the set of behaviors and practices, by travelers and providers alike, that can lead to sustainable tourism. It aims to maximize benefits to local communities and minimize social and environmental harm. Both service providers and consumers are held accountable for the tourism they develop or join. Some critics argue it distracts from wider issues that need regulation, such as visitor numbers and environmental impact.

nature-es-023.title: Fractal fluency: eyes tuned to nature's patterns
nature-es-023.text: Clouds, mountains and trees are natural fractals, patterns that repeat at different scales. Fractal fluency is a neuroscience model holding that human vision has adapted to process such patterns with ease. People handle fractals with a fractal dimension between 1.3 and 1.5 especially well, and viewing them lowers physical stress and boosts thinking. Because people spend 92% of their time indoors, designers now build nature-like fractals into buildings.

nature-es-024.title: Kinship with nature in Indigenous cultures
nature-es-024.text: Before harvesting wild rice, the Anishinaabe make offerings. The act reflects a view common in many Indigenous cultures: humans are part of the natural world, bound to it by kinship and reciprocity. Humans, animals, plants and soil depend on each other for survival and health. This view underlies {{ref:nature-gov-176}}, such as the controlled burns used by some Native American and Aboriginal Australian societies. Indigenous and animist beliefs usually treat nature as sacred.

nature-es-035.title: Sacred natural sites: groves the gods protected
nature-es-035.text: India alone has at least 13,720 reported sacred groves, with an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 in total. A sacred natural site is a natural feature or area of land or water with special spiritual meaning for a people or community. Such sites include mountains, forests, groves, trees, rivers, lakes, caves, islands and springs, from a single tree to whole mountain ranges. They exist on every continent except Antarctica. Many have been protected for long periods with little use, and some are notably rich in biodiversity. Beyond sheltering species, they can supply water, medicines and other ecosystem services and support pilgrimage and tourism. They should not be romanticized, though: some have been governed by taboos that exclude women or marginalized groups. The {{ref:nature-gov-015}} recognized an urgent need to protect them and in 2004 issued the Akwe Kon guidelines for assessing developments that may affect them.

nature-es-041.title: How many visitors is too many?
nature-es-041.text: Peru limits hikers on the Inca Trail to 500 a day, because geologists warned that more could cause serious erosion. That cap rests on tourism carrying capacity. It is the most visitors a place can take at once without harming its environment, economy or community, or spoiling the experience. The idea came from wildlife and range management. Physical capacity is how many people fit, usually at around 1m per person. Social capacity is exceeded when local tolerance falls, enjoyment drops and crime rises. Biophysical capacity is passed when damage outruns a habitat's ability to regenerate. Economic capacity can mark where tourism revenue is overtaken by the inflation tourism causes. How much damage is acceptable is a human judgment; where pristine conditions are the goal, capacity may be zero. Several authors argue the concept is flawed in theory and practice. It assumes stable systems and is hard to calculate, and UNESCO warns it can make a site look better protected than it is. Frameworks built around management objectives have largely replaced it.

nature-es-013.title: Keeping ecotourism honest
nature-es-013.text: Ecotourism operators sell places they could easily damage, so managers use a toolkit to protect them. It includes setting a carrying capacity, hardening sites against wear, sustainable design, visitor quotas, fees, access limits and visitor education. Labels such as the European Ecotourism Labelling Standard try to certify genuine low-impact operators. Recognition matters: when responsible operators go unrecognized, they lose out to rivals that only claim to be green.

nature-es-037.title: The happiness set point
nature-es-037.text: Happiness may be partly built in. Set point theory holds that each person has an inherited baseline level of subjective well-being. Top-down theories see a genetic tendency to be happy or unhappy that fixes this setpoint. Personality studies find genetics account for 20–48% of the variance in the Five-Factor personality traits, and the variance in subjective well-being is also heritable.

nature-es-016.title: Beautiful, sublime or picturesque
nature-es-016.text: Philosophers once sorted the appreciation of nature into three kinds. The beautiful is the tame beauty of gardens, small, smooth and fair in color. The sublime is the awe of wild, threatening nature, powerful, intense and terrifying. The picturesque mixes the two, seeing nature as scenes like pictures: varied, irregular, rich and forceful. Viewed with disinterest, mountains and wilderness can be admired rather than feared.

nature-es-019.title: Are people losing touch with nature?
nature-es-019.text: One review concluded that within a generation children's lives have largely moved indoors. That matters, because childhood experience of nature builds lifelong care for it. Indoor lifestyles and rising screen time have cut human contact with nature, and earlier studies link the decline to effects on health and care for the environment. Yet a global review found the evidence still too thin to judge how large or general the decline is.

nature-es-021.title: Nature on prescription
nature-es-021.text: Since 2019, general practitioners in the UK have referred patients to the NHS-funded Dose of Nature program. Nature prescriptions are health-system programs in which doctors or public agencies formally send people to spend time in nature. Canada lets physicians formally prescribe it. Dose of Nature claimed a 64% recovery rate for its first 1500 patients, against 50% for talk therapy. Finnish researchers recommend about five hours a month in nature as preventive health care.

nature-es-018.title: Measuring a bond with nature
nature-es-018.text: At least seventeen scales measure nature connectedness. One of the most used is the nature relatedness scale, a 21-item questionnaire that measures how connected to nature a person feels as a lasting trait. Its three subscales cover identifying with nature, concern about human effects on the environment, and comfort and wish to be in nature. It is reliable, with alpha = .87, and stable when retested six months later, alpha = .85.

nature-es-032.title: City parks and mental health
nature-es-032.text: Residents living 800m to 1.6km from a park had mental health scores 4.5 points lower than those within 400m of one. City parks help reduce stress and lower the risk of anxiety and depression for people living near them. They are cheap and open to all. That makes their mental health benefits available regardless of income or background.

nature-es-029.title: Placelessness: places that could be anywhere
nature-es-029.text: Strip malls, gas stations, fast food chains and chain stores share an odd quality: they feel as if they could be anywhere. Cultural geographer Edward Relph called this placelessness, the lack of a sense of place. Anthropologist Marc Augé called such locations non-places. Even historic districts can drift this way when they are heavily commercialized for tourism.

nature-es-045.title: Stress recovery: nature calms the body
nature-es-045.text: Stress recovery theory holds that contact with nature helps the body and emotions recover from stress, lowering cortisol and heart rate. It usually appears alongside attention restoration theory, and the two describe complementary ways nature may benefit well-being. The benefits of nature therapy are usually linked to this recovery. Managing city trees has been shown to promote stress recovery and psychological healing.

nature-es-042.title: Limits of acceptable change: managing by goals, not head counts
nature-es-042.text: In the 1980s the US Forest Service developed the limits of acceptable change, the first framework to follow carrying capacity. Instead of a single maximum visitor number, it monitors a site against set objectives. It assumes any tourist activity has some impact, so a visitor cap is only one tool among many. It is often summarized as a nine-step process, from choosing indicators of resource and social conditions to selecting preferred management options.

openers.cultural-services-and-human-wellbeing: Not every gift from nature can be eaten, drunk or burned. This chapter turns to the services that work on the mind: recreation done for pleasure, outdoor pursuits in wild settings, and the beauty that philosophers of nature have studied for centuries. It asks whether humans carry an inborn urge to connect with living things, and how far people count nature as part of who they are. Behind it all sits one question: what makes a life go well, judged both by philosophers and by people themselves? The chapter also follows the money into nature tourism and ecotourism, and asks who really keeps the gains when multinational companies run the show.

reviews.cultural-services-and-human-wellbeing: Cultural services are the ones felt rather than harvested: recreation, beauty, a sense of place and the spiritual meaning of a sacred grove. The evidence that they shape well-being keeps growing, from Danish children raised among green space to students who erred less after glimpsing a flowering roof for 40 seconds. Theories compete to explain why, through restored attention, recovery from stress or an inborn love of living things. These benefits also carry a price tag, with outdoor recreation alone worth 2.4 percent of US GDP, and tourism turns them into a business that can protect places or wear them out. Carrying capacities, certification labels and the limits of acceptable change are attempts to keep enjoyment of nature from destroying what people came to enjoy.
